walkthrough.brief:
# AmberX AXF investor tour

## Prompt (verbatim)

> Run a chain to demonstrate and explain these features for an investor demo.

## Shape

- Audience: investors. Investors: lead with the value and what is unique, keep jargon out, show it working, one idea per step.
- Style: showcase; depth: standard (about 5 steps per feature).
- Try it: every feature ends with a step the viewer does themselves.
- Plays in: console, recorded ahead of time, no live model during playback.

## Features (5)

1. **Asset (asset@1)** (concept, `concept:asset`): A JSON file in the one shared asset@1 format that describes a visible piece of the UI: a theme, layout, menu, toolbar, dialog, button, slider, container or access policy.
2. **Theme manager** (plugin, `plugin:theme-manager`): Roll colour, style and layout themes, or every themeable part at once.
3. **Only undescribed** (setting, `control:console-web:glossary-index:only-undescribed`): Shows only entries whose source has no description of its own, so you can see what still needs writing.
4. **Build orchestrator** (plugin, `plugin:build-orchestrator`): Breaks every build into small steps (30 min or less), each pinned to Fable or Opus.
5. **Merge queue** (concept, `concept:merge-queue`): The only way a pull request reaches main: ready PRs are stacked, tested once on top of main plus the PRs ahead, and merged without a retest when green.

## Each feature answers

```json
{
  "headline": "one line: why this matters",
  "points": ["2-5 short documentation points"],
  "steps": [{ "kind": "narrate|show|try|docs", "title": "short", "say": "what the narrator says", "do": "console action or empty", "target": "element to highlight or empty", "highlight": "label on the highlight" }]
}
```

intro.title: AmberX AXF investor tour
intro.say: Welcome. This walkthrough shows Asset (asset@1), Theme manager, Only undescribed, Build orchestrator and Merge queue. Each part shows it working, then lets you try it. Use Next and Back any time.

outro.title: That is the tour
outro.say: That was Asset (asset@1), Theme manager, Only undescribed, Build orchestrator and Merge queue. Open any part again from the list, or read its docs.

docs.headline: Every visible piece of the product is data, so the look changes without touching code.
docs.summary: A JSON file in the one shared asset@1 format that describes a visible piece of the UI: a theme, layout, menu, toolbar, dialog, button, slider, container or access policy.
docs.detail: Every asset has $axf, type, id, name, version, description, author, tags and data. Engines compile assets into tokens and CSS variables; the UI reads only those tokens, so swapping an asset restyles every app with no code change.
points: One shared JSON format, asset@1, describes themes, layouts, menus, toolbars, dialogs, buttons and access policies.
Engines compile assets into design tokens; screens read only those tokens.
Swap an asset and every app built on the framework restyles at once, with no code change.
The same assets drive the web port and the Android port.

steps.title: Everything is an asset
steps.say: Start with the idea the whole product is built on. Every piece of the interface you see is an asset: a small JSON file in one shared format.

steps.title: Data, not code
steps.say: A theme, a menu, a toolbar, even who may press which button, is described as data. Engines turn that data into design tokens, and the screens read only those tokens.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.say: That means the look of every app can change without a developer touching code, and one change reaches every app on the framework.

steps.title: Try it
steps.say: Your turn: think of one screen you would restyle for a customer. Tap Next and we will do it live.

docs.headline: Restyle the whole product live, in seconds, safely.
docs.summary: Roll colour, style and layout themes, or every themeable part at once.
docs.detail: Roll colour, style and layout themes, or every themeable part at once. A tree of every token (built from the asset types, so new types show up by themselves) with tri-state ticks, locks, presets and search picks what a roll may change; rolls stay readable (contrast-checked palettes, sizes within the range the known themes use). Live preview, undo/redo, pin favourites, edit any value by hand, save a roll as standard asset@1 themes and manage them (apply, rename, duplicate, export, import, delete). Phone: drill-down tree. Nav → Plugins → Theme manager; Settings → Plugins → Themes.
points: Roll new colour, style and layout themes, or every themeable part at once.
Rolls stay readable: palettes are contrast-checked and sizes stay in range.
Live preview with undo and redo; pin the ones you like.
Save a roll as a standard theme asset and apply it everywhere.

steps.title: The Theme manager
steps.say: This is the Theme manager. It is where the look of the product is changed while it runs.

steps.title: Roll a new look
steps.say: Roll new colours, styles and layouts, or everything at once. Every roll is checked for contrast, so it stays readable.

steps.title: Safe to experiment
steps.say: There is a live preview with undo and redo. Keep the looks you like, and save one as a theme asset for every app.

steps.title: Try it
steps.say: Your turn: roll a theme here and watch the whole console change. Tap Next when you are done.

docs.headline: The product documents itself: thousands of entries, built from the code, and the gaps are measured.
docs.summary: Shows only entries whose source has no description of its own, so you can see what still needs writing.
docs.detail: Shows only entries whose source has no description of its own, so you can see what still needs writing. Their summary is generated.
points: The glossary is rebuilt from what the code registers: plugins, screens, controls, settings, commands and assets.
Every entry says what it is, where it appears, its API and what it links to.
Continuous integration fails if anything new has no entry, and the number still undescribed may only go down.
This walkthrough was generated from those entries.

steps.title: The encyclopedia
steps.say: This is the glossary: an encyclopedia of the whole product, built from the code itself, so it never goes out of date.

steps.title: Built from the code
steps.say: Every plugin, screen, control, setting and command gets an entry automatically. If something new ships without one, the build fails.

steps.title: Gaps are measured
steps.say: Only undescribed shows the entries that still need their own words. That number is tracked, and it is only allowed to go down.

steps.title: Try it
steps.say: Your turn: switch on Only undescribed and see what is left to write.

docs.headline: AI builds the product in small, tracked, reviewable steps.
docs.summary: Breaks every build into small steps (30 min or less), each pinned to Fable or Opus.
docs.detail: Breaks every build into small steps (30 min or less), each pinned to Fable or Opus. Consecutive same-model steps form a phase; a phase that switches model waits for Brett's approval. Token rules on every build: one session, no sub-agents unless a step allows it, briefs carry only the current phase. Page = tab group (Builds, Approvals, Rules); the Builds tab looks and behaves like Pending builds, with more options (per-step model, phases, approve switch, next-phase brief, hide, archive, import from Pending, move/edit/remove steps). Tracker is a repo file, _claude/builds/orchestrator.json, so any session or account continues the build (orchestrator.mjs next | brief | act).
points: Every build is split into steps of 30 minutes or less.
Each step is pinned to the right AI model for the job.
Progress is stored in the repository, so any session can pick up where another left off.
Reachable from the console, over REST and as MCP tools.

steps.title: The Build orchestrator
steps.say: This is the Build orchestrator, where every piece of work on the product is planned and tracked.

steps.title: Small steps
steps.say: Every build is broken into steps of thirty minutes or less, and each step is pinned to the AI model best suited to it.

steps.title: Nothing gets lost
steps.say: Progress lives in the repository itself, so any session, on any machine, can continue a build exactly where the last one stopped.

steps.title: Try it
steps.say: Your turn: open any build in the list and look at its steps. Tap Next when you are ready.

docs.headline: Changes land safely and cheaply: tested once, merged together.
docs.summary: The only way a pull request reaches main: ready PRs are stacked, tested once on top of main plus the PRs ahead, and merged without a retest when green.
points: Every change reaches main only through the merge queue.
Ready changes are stacked and each is tested once on top of the ones ahead.
Green changes merge with no retest; a failing one is removed and the rest carry on.
Fewer test runs means less compute spent.

steps.title: The merge queue
steps.say: Last, how changes reach the product. Nothing lands on the main line except through the merge queue.

steps.title: Tested once
steps.say: Ready changes are stacked and tested once, together. Green ones merge without testing again, and a failing one is simply taken out.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.say: That keeps the product stable while many AI builds run at the same time, and it saves compute on every release.

steps.title: Your take
steps.say: Your turn: picture ten builds finishing at once. The queue lands them safely, one stack, one test run. Tap Next to finish.

history.note: Written by Claude (Opus 5.5) ahead of time
